analysis.one_liner: Requires coal-fired power plants and other major mercury emitters to cut mercury emissions by at least 95 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee in 1999; no vote was ever held, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force fossil fuel power plants, industrial boilers, waste incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and cement plants to cut their mercury emissions by at least 95 percent, with monitoring, permits, and public reporting of each facility's emissions. It would also have required mercury-containing products like batteries and fluorescent bulbs to be labeled, pulled out of the trash stream, and phased out of sale unless a manufacturer proved no mercury-free alternative existed. The stated aim was to reduce mercury that settles into lakes and rivers and ends up in fish eaten by pregnant women, children, and others.
analysis.who_benefits: People who eat fish from contaminated waters, pregnant women and their fetuses, children, and communities near coal plants, incinerators, and chemical plants. EPA's own report, cited in the bill, found the highest mercury deposition in the Great Lakes, Ohio River Valley, and Northeast, and 39 states had issued warnings about mercury-tainted fish by 1997.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered power plant, boiler, incinerator, chlor-alkali plant, and cement plant to cut annual mercury emissions by at least 95 percent below its baseline.
Requires enforceable permits, monitoring every 90 days, and annual public reporting of facility-specific mercury emissions, so residents can see what nearby plants are releasing.
Requires mercury captured by pollution controls to be disposed of so it cannot leak into groundwater, surface water, or soil.

Bans the sale of mercury-containing products after three years unless the manufacturer wins an exemption proving the use is essential, no affordable mercury-free alternative exists, and a take-back recycling program is in place.

Requires labeling of mercury-containing products, separation of those items from the solid waste stream before incineration or landfilling, and better, more consistent fish consumption advisories across states.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal- and oil-fired power plants and industrial boilers, municipal and private waste incinerators, mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants, and Portland cement plants would bear the cost of controls, monitoring, and permits. Some of those costs could pass through to electricity customers and to buyers of cement and chlorine products. Manufacturers of mercury-containing batteries, lamps, and instruments would face labeling, take-back, and phaseout requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plants, incinerators, cement and chemical makers

drawbacks.text: A flat 95 percent reduction for every unit, with trading allowed only among units at a single site, would be expensive and possibly impractical for some plants, and those costs could flow to electricity ratepayers and industrial customers.

The bill required EPA to write the rules within 180 days and units to obtain compliant permits within two years — a very fast schedule that could strain both regulators and smaller operators, including municipal incinerators.

The three-year phaseout of mercury-containing products would raise costs for some medical, scientific, and electrical equipment users until mercury-free substitutes became available at reasonable cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Mercury is a potent neurotoxin, and the bill targeted the specific sources EPA had identified as the largest emitters while building in cost flexibility (site-level trading, multiple control methods, narrow exemptions). The main honest objection is the speed and rigidity of the 95 percent target, which could have driven higher electricity prices in coal-dependent regions. The public-health upside — fewer fish advisories, less mercury reaching fetuses and children — was the bill's central promise, and it died before anyone had to weigh that trade-off in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to the Health and Environment Subcommittee a month later, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Allen of Maine introduced the bill on August 2, 1999, with 28 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day.

On September 10, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where legislation of this kind typically waits for the full committee to act; the full committee never advanced it.
No further action appears in the bill's history, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plants, waste incinerators, chlor-alkali plants, and cement plants were better off because the bill never advanced, since they faced no new 95 percent mercury reduction mandate. Communities in the Great Lakes, Ohio River Valley, and Northeast regions the bill identified as mercury hotspots continued to bear the exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mercury-emitting plants and their trade groups

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Allen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 30 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 26 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee for a markup or scheduled it for a House vote; it sat at the subcommittee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: Support leaned Democratic: 26 of the 30 cosponsors were Democrats, with 3 Republicans and 1 Independent, and no committee or floor action ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have required a 95 percent cut in mercury emissions from every power plant, the largest single source of U.S. mercury emissions per the EPA report the bill cites. Compliance costs could pass to ratepayers, but the emissions fall on nearby communities and waterways.

These plants use mercury directly in production and would have had to cut direct and fugitive mercury emissions by 95 percent or change processes, which in practice pushes toward non-mercury technology.
Cement kilns would have faced 95 percent mercury reduction requirements for direct and fugitive dust emissions, plus permitting and monitoring costs.

industries.industry: Waste incineration and medical/hazardous waste disposal
industries.note: Incinerators would face a strict emission rate ceiling, mandatory control equipment if they exceeded it, and monitoring and reporting duties; municipal incinerators in particular would bear costs, while residents near incinerators would get cleaner air.

industries.industry: Battery, fluorescent lamp, and instrument manufacturers
industries.note: The bill required labeling, take-back programs, and eventually a phaseout of mercury-containing products unless no mercury-free alternative existed at reasonable cost. Some makers would have to reformulate; others would see their mercury-based products restricted.
